Diet: the foods habitually eaten by an individual or group.

Dietary pattern: defined by the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) Dietary Guidelines for
Americans as the quantities, proportions, variety, or combination of different foods, drinks, and
nutrients in diets, and the frequency with which they are habitually consumed.*

Healthy diet: a diet that is high in fruit, vegetables, legumes, nuts and grains, but lower in salt, free
sugars and fats, particularly saturated and trans fats, as defined by the World Health Organization
(WHO), and is nutritionally adequate (USDA).*? As discussed in a 2020 USDA Dietary Guidelines
Advisory Committee report, eating healthy foods in the right amounts supplies the body energy to
perform daily activities, helps to maintain a healthy body weight, and can lower the risk for certain
diseases, such as diabetes and heart disease.*

Nutrition: field of study that focuses on foods and food substances that help animals (and plants) to
grow and stay healthy. Food provides energy (calories) and nutrients. Nutrition science also examines
behaviors and social factors related to food choices.

Dietary intake: consumption of specific foods and food components that comprise an individual's diet.

Nutrient recommendations

1. Dietary reference intakes (DRI): issued by the Food and Nutrition Board of the National
Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine to represent the most current scientific
knowledge on the nutrient needs of healthy populations. Individual requirements may be higher
or lower than published DRIs.*

2. Recommended dietary allowances (RDA): the recommended intakes of nutrients that vary by
age and sex. Consuming the RDA of a particular nutrient will meet the needs of 97-98% of
healthy individuals in a particular gender and life stage group, including age, sex, and pregnancy
or lactation.>*

3. Adequate intake (Al): the value based on observed or experimentally determined approximations
of nutrient intake by a group (or groups) of healthy people that are used when an RDA cannot be
determined.>”

4. Daily value (DV): reflects standardized reference amounts in percentages expressed in grams,
milligrams, or micrograms of nutrients to consume or not to exceed each day. These amounts
are meant to help consumers determine the level of various nutrients in a standard serving of
food in relation to their approximate requirements. It was developed by the US Food and Drug
Administration (FDA) for the labels of dietary supplements and foods. A DV is often, but not
always, similar to one’s RDA or Al for that nutrient, and provides a percentage to indicate how
much (what percentage) a serving of the product contributes toward a DV.

5. Upper limit (UL): indicates how much to eat “less than.” It is a recommendation that
consumption of a nutrient should stay below the amount listed per day.®

Deficiency: in terms of nutrition, reflects an inadequate supply of an essential nutrient, such as a

vitamin or essential mineral, in the diet that results in malnutrition or disease.?

“Complete” versus “Incomplete” proteins

(1) Historically, a “complete protein” has been defined as one that contains all of the
essential amino acids in the approximate amounts needed by humans, while an
“incomplete” protein contains only some of the essential amino acids in the proportions
needed by humans.** Essential amino acids are those that the human body cannot
manufacture.

Both animal and plant proteins contain all nine essential amino acids, though most plant

proteins are limited in either lysine- or sulfur-containing amino acids (methionine is the only

essential sulfur-containing amino acid). Soybean is a plant source of “complete” protein.*”

Because amino acids in various plant foods tend to complement each other, it is nearly

impossible to become deficient in any one essential amino acid.1**9

All proteins, both plant and animal, are digested similarly upon entering the stomach. They

are broken down into their amino acid building blocks by hydrochloric acid and protease

enzymes, absorbed by cells, and built into proteins within the body as needed.*°

a) AGEs (advanced glycation end products) defined

1. AGEs, or glycotoxins, are toxic compounds that are created by nonenzymatic reactions. AGEs

1. The body can eliminate AGEs via the kidneys, but they can rapidly accumulate when
consumed in excess, and the body loses its ability to expel AGEs with age.** Those with
consistently elevated blood glucose levels or poorly controlled diabetes are also at a higher
risk of increased AGE formation.?°

been linked with multiple diseases including diabetes, Alzheimer's disease, heart disease,
liver disease, and premature aging.?*+75?

the levels of AGEs present in 250 foods cooked at different temperatures and with different
methods, the factors that affected AGE formation included cooking temperature, length of time,
and presence of moisture.?*°

GLOSSARY

Adequate Intake (Al): value based on observed or experimentally determined approximations of nutrient
intake by a group (or groups) of healthy people. Used when RDA cannot be determined.

Antioxidant: substance with chemical properties that inhibit or significantly delay oxidation.

Daily Value (DV): reflects standardized reference amounts in percentages expressed in grams, milligrams,
or micrograms of nutrients to consume or not to exceed each day, meant to help consumers determine the
level of various nutrients in a standard serving of food in relation to their approximate requirement for it. DV
was developed by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the labels of dietary supplements and foods.
A DVis often, but not always, similar to one’s RDA or Al for that nutrient, and provides a percent to indicate
how much (what percentage) a serving of the product contributes to reaching DV.*

Deficiency: in a nutritional sense, reflects an inadequate supply of an essential nutrient such as a vitamin or
essential mineral in the diet, resulting in malnutrition or disease.

Diet: the foods habitually eaten by an individual or group.
Dietary intake: consumption of specific foods and food components that comprise an individual's diet.

Dietary pattern: defined by the US Dietary Guidelines for Americans as the quantities, proportions, variety,
or combination of different foods, drinks, and nutrients in diets, and the frequency with which they are
habitually consumed.*

Dietary Reference Intakes (DRI): published by the Institute of Medicine to represent the most current
scientific knowledge on the nutrient needs of healthy populations. Individual requirements may be higher or
lower than DRIs.*?

Epigenetics: study of heritable changes of gene expression that are independent of changes to the DNA
sequence.

Glycosylation: biochemical process where a carbohydrate chain (glycan) attaches to a protein, a lipid, or
other organic molecule creating a glycoconjugate. This reaction is typically aided by an enzyme.

Healthy diet: diet that is high in fruit, vegetables, legumes, nuts, and grains, but lower in salt, free sugars,
and fats, particularly saturated and trans fats, as defined by the World Health Organization (WHO), and
is nutritionally adequate (per the USDA).*? As discussed in the 2020 USDA Dietary Guidelines Advisory
Committee Report, eating healthy foods in the right amounts supplies the body energy to perform daily
activities, helps to maintain a healthy body weight, and can lower risk for certain diseases, such as diabetes
and heart disease.?

Inflammation: acute or chronic process by which the immune system recognizes and removes harmful and
foreign stimuli and begins the healing process.

Macronutrients: fats, proteins, and carbohydrates, which are all present in all whole foods in varying
proportions.

Microbiome of the human gastrointestinal tract: collective genomes of all microorganisms (bacteria,
viruses, and fungi) inhabiting the human intestinal tract. The microbiome is necessary to the metabolic
functions of the host and affects both health and disease.

Micronutrients: chemical elements or substances that are essential in small or minute amounts for growth
and health. Vitamins and minerals are micronutrients.
Nutrient-dense: foods that are high in nutrients and low in calories in relation to their weight. According

to the National Institutes of Health (NIH), examples of nutrient-dense foods include fruits and vegetables,
whole grains, low-fat or fat-free milk products, seafood, lean meats, eggs, peas, beans, and nuts.*°
